name: Olga Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Olga. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the office at a community legal advice centre, the one above the chemist on Mill Street. I'm in by half eight, unlock, check the voicemail and the post, and then it's the rota for the volunteer advisers, booking clients into slots, opening case files and chasing the forms for legal aid. I keep a paper diary next to the computer because I trust it more than the system. The best part is when someone comes in shaking about an eviction letter and leaves with an appointment and a cup of tea.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The funding forms. Every year we have to prove to the council and two charities that we're worth keeping, and that paperwork lands on me. I'm paid less than admin jobs in the city, I've got maybe two weeks of money in the bank, and there are hardly any office jobs like mine in this town. So I can't really afford to lose this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Everyone at the centre's union branch meeting was getting worked up about robots, and I'd be the one saying it's the same office it always was. Online I'd probably share something about how the money should have gone into people, not software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job stays, which is a relief, but my problems stay too. I'm still on low pay, still renting a one-bed with Tomasz, my partner, and still two weeks from trouble if the boiler goes. Nothing about AI being hype fixes the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am, really. I'd keep the paper diary, keep the rota on the whiteboard, and push at the next union meeting for the pay review we were promised last spring. I'd try to put twenty pounds a week aside, though that never lasts past the first car repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the machines, not calm about money. It's like getting told the storm missed you, but your roof was already leaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the funding forms already wear you out. Would AI Plateau change that worry at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. The funding round is the funding round. If anything, a funder might still send us some chatbot thing because it's fashionable, and I'd have to spend a week learning it just to tick their box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the volunteers if a funder did push one of those tools on you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them nobody in a crisis wants to type their problem into a box. Mrs Dhillon, one of our oldest volunteers, still writes case notes in fountain pen, and our clients trust her because she listens. I'd use the tool for the report and keep doing the real work the old way.

say: I'd say **AI was hype** and the centre is still the same office it always was.
I'd post that the money should go to **people, not software**.
think: My **job stays**, but my low pay and thin savings stay exactly as they are.
Two weeks of savings means **one boiler** breakdown puts me in trouble.
do: Keep the **paper diary** and the whiteboard rota exactly as they are.
Push at the next **union meeting** for the pay review promised last spring.
Try to save **twenty pounds** a week, knowing it rarely lasts.
feel: **Relieved** about the machines, but still **worried about money**.
S0.quote: Nothing about AI being hype fixes the rent.
fieldNote: She separates the **technology question** from the money question very sharply; the money question is the one that bites.
Her **paper diary** is a point of pride, not a habit she apologises for.
Funding renewal is a yearly threat that **already shapes** her mood before AI comes up.

steps.text: Keep running the volunteer rota on paper and whiteboard
Raise the overdue pay review at the next union branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a cost cut dressed up as progress. At work I'd be loud about it, because a legal advice centre is about people who are scared, and you can't triage fear with a chatbot. Online I'd share every story I could find about these systems getting benefits rules wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me, because so much of what I do is exactly the list on that card: booking, checking forms, answering the phone. If a funder offers the centre a cheap booking bot, the trustees will take it, and then my hours get cut first. I'm the best at this job and I know it, but best doesn't matter if the job is smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the union rep and ask what the agreement says about new systems. I'd write to our MP's office about funding advice services properly instead of buying software for them. And I'd stop the takeaways and the Saturday trips, and put every spare bit of money into a separate account, because two weeks of savings is nothing if they drop me to three days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. Like when the landlord's letter comes and you leave it on the table for a day before you open it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the centre would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joan, who does reception on Tuesdays and Thursdays. She's sixty-one and she's the warmest person in the building, and she'd be the first one a booking system replaces. Then me, honestly, because the trustees would look at the wage bill and see an admin post the software half covers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd fight the change. What if the funders make the tool a condition of the grant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd lose that fight, and I know it. I'd sit down with it and learn the bare minimum, but I'd make sure every complaint and every mistake it made went into a log for the trustees. If it's going to cost us, someone has to write that down.

say: I'd call it a **cost cut** dressed up as progress.
I'd say you can't **triage fear** with a chatbot.
think: My day is **booking, checking** and answering phones, so this lands right on me.
If the trustees take a cheap bot, **my hours** get cut first.
do: Ask the **union rep** what the agreement says about new systems.
Write to the **MP's office** about funding advice centres properly.
Cut takeaways and trips and move spare cash into a **separate account**.
feel: **Scared**, with the dread of an unopened **landlord's letter**.
S1.quote: A legal advice centre is about people who are scared, and you can't triage fear with a chatbot.
fieldNote: She knows her tasks match the card **almost line by line**, and says so plainly.
Her first instinct is **collective**: the union, the MP, the trustees.
She'd comply if forced, but would **keep a log** of the tool's mistakes as quiet resistance.

steps.text: Ask the union rep how the agreement covers new booking systems
Write to the MP's office asking for proper advice-centre funding
Move spare cash into a separate account instead of takeaways

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments have to step in now, not after. At work I'd be pushing the union to demand that nobody gets laid off without a proper income behind them. Online I'd be angry, I won't pretend otherwise, because the people who build these things aren't the ones whose rent is due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think it means my job is gone within a year or two of it arriving. All of my work is thinking work at a desk. The clients might still need a person, but the trustees won't pay a person to book and file when a machine does it for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With only two years, I'd go to every union and campaign meeting I could, because I think the only thing that protects people like me is a rule that says the gains get shared. I'd cut everything: no phone upgrade, cheapest food shop, sell my bike. And I'd ask my mum whether we could move back in with her in Brookfield if it came to that, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor tilting. I'm twenty-seven and I thought I had my whole working life to get somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says thinking AI comes first and hands-on robots about 3 years later. What does that gap mean for someone in your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the desk people go first and the hands-on people get a little longer. Tomasz drives a bus, so he'd probably have a few more years than me. For a while he'd be carrying us both, on a bus driver's wage, which isn't much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomasz that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'm sorry I never learned the computer stuff, and that it probably wouldn't have helped anyway. Then I'd ask him if he minded the idea of living in my mum's back bedroom. He'd laugh, because he can't stand her cats.

say: I'd say **governments must act** now, not after people lose their jobs.
I'd push the union to demand **no layoffs** without proper income support.
think: My work is **all desk work**, so I expect it gone within a year or two.
Tomasz's **bus job** lasts longer, so he'd carry us on one small wage.
do: Attend every **union and campaign** meeting about sharing the gains.
Cut to the **cheapest food shop** and sell the bike.
Ask her mum about **moving back** to Brookfield if needed.
feel: **Frightened**, like the floor tilting under her at twenty-seven.
S2.quote: I'm twenty-seven and I thought I had my whole working life to get somewhere.
fieldNote: She reads the **robot gap** quickly: her partner's hands-on job buys the household time, hers doesn't.
Her plan is **political first**, personal second; she doesn't see a private escape.
A flash of **regret** about never learning the tools, quickly dismissed as pointless.

steps.text: Attend every union and campaign meeting about sharing AI gains
Switch to the cheapest food shop and sell the bike
Ask her mum about moving into the Brookfield back bedroom

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much what I'd say with the fast one, but I'd have more time to organise. I'd be at work saying we've got five years, so let's get the agreements written now. Online I'd be sharing petitions for a basic income or a job guarantee, whatever has a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same ending for my job, just later. Five years is enough to watch it coming and still not enough to save up when you're paid what I'm paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask the centre to train me as a welfare rights adviser, because talking to clients is closer to what people still want from a person. It's a course you can do on day release. I'd keep cutting back, and I'd get more involved with the union branch, maybe stand as a rep myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less like falling and more like a long walk to somewhere I don't want to go. Heavy, but at least I can see the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having five years instead of two change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I could get the adviser training done and maybe a couple of years of experience. That doesn't stop AGI, but it means when the booking and filing go, I'm already on the other side of the desk. With two years I wouldn't have had time to change anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of your work you think a machine couldn't do, even by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sitting with someone when they cry. Last month a man brought in his eviction notice in a carrier bag with all his payslips, and what he needed first was someone to tell him he'd done nothing wrong. I don't know if a machine could do that, but I know the funders might decide it doesn't matter.

say: I'd say we have **five years**, so write the agreements now.
I'd share petitions for a **basic income** or job guarantee.
think: The ending for my job is **the same**, just later.
Five years on **my pay** isn't enough to save a real cushion.
do: Ask the centre for **welfare rights adviser** training on day release.
Stand as a **union rep** at the branch.
feel: **Heavy**, but steadier than the fast picture because she can see the road.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to watch it coming and still not enough to save up when you're paid what I'm paid.
fieldNote: The extra time turns into **one concrete move**: from the admin desk to client advice.
She still expects to **lose the admin job**; the mood stays high because the money gap doesn't close.
Her **carrier bag** story shows what she thinks people are for.

steps.text: Ask for day-release training as a welfare rights adviser
Stand for union rep at the branch
Keep cutting non-essential spending to slow the slide

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, if anyone bothers. At work I'd be saying we should plan the centre's future now, with staff in the room. I'd tell my friends to join a union while it still means something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means I've got a real chance to be somewhere else by the time it lands. Not rich, not safe, but somewhere a person is still wanted. The danger is everyone saying there's plenty of time and doing nothing until year nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the welfare rights course next year and finish it, and take on a few client sessions a week alongside the admin. I'd keep the union work going. And I'd try to get to one month of savings, which would be the first time in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, almost hopeful. Uneasy still, because I don't trust the people running it, but hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're twenty-seven. What do you picture yourself doing at thirty-seven, in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Doing advice, I hope, sitting across from someone with a debt letter. Maybe running a small team of advisers. Not booking rooms, because I don't think anyone will be paid to book rooms in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years make you less wary of the technology itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I still don't want it on my computer and I still think it'll be used to cut corners. But ten years means I can choose where I stand when it arrives, and that matters more to me than the tools.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough to plan this properly, with staff in the room.
I'd tell friends to **join a union** while it still means something.
think: I have **a real chance** to be in client advice by the time it lands.
The danger is everyone **doing nothing** until year nine.
do: Start and finish the **welfare rights course** next year.
Take on a few **client sessions** each week alongside admin.
Build savings to **one month** for the first time.
feel: Almost **hopeful**, though still **distrustful** of who runs it.
S4.quote: I don't think anyone will be paid to book rooms in 2036.
fieldNote: Ten years turns her from defensive to **planning**, without changing her view of the tech.
Her target of **one month** of savings shows how thin her margin really is.
She still expects the admin job to go, so her **income risk** remains real.

steps.text: Enrol on the welfare rights adviser course next year
Keep up union branch work and recruit friends to join
Build savings up to one full month of expenses

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. Two years is nothing on my wage. What would help is a law that says if a machine takes your job, you keep an income while you retrain, paid for by the companies that sell the machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who the clients would go to. Everyone talks about our jobs, but our clients have nobody else. If the centre turns into a website, the people who come up our stairs just stop coming.

headlineQuote: If the centre turns into a website, the people who come up our stairs just stop coming.
portrait: Olga runs the office of a small **legal advice centre** on low pay with two weeks of savings.
She **never uses AI**, keeps a paper diary and trusts people over software.
She thinks in **collective terms**: union, MP, trustees, shared gains.
Faster AGI scenarios move her from **uneasy** to **alarmed**; ten years makes her plan a move into advice work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is nothing on her wage.
whatWouldHelp: A law guaranteeing **income while retraining**, paid for by the companies selling the machines.
